newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST-Spain inflation to fall again in Dec, Jan.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Spain inflation to fall again in Dec, Jan.

text.p: Better-than-expected November inflation data have paved the way for Spain's Consumer Price Index to undershoot its official 1996 target of a 3.4 percent rise, analysts said on Friday.
Indeed November's CPI suggested that inflation may well be below three percent in early 1997, they added.
"In December we may have both the core and the general rate at 3.1 percent," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
The CPI was unchanged in November from October, and up 3.2 percent year-on-year versus 3.5 percent the previous month. Core inflation was unchanged on the month and up 3.1 percent year-on-year.
Analysts on average had expected November inflation to decline to 3.3 percent, with core inflation at 3.2 percent.

The lower-than-expected rise was announced shortly before the Bank of Spain's decision to cut its key money market rate for the seventh time this year, lopping off 50 basis points to leave it at 6.25 percent.

"Core inflation was the most surprising. This is a historic fact --the first time it was unchanged in November and with a yearly rise of 3.1 percent," said Banco Bilbao Vizcaya's chief economist Miguel Sebastian.
November's CPI may indicate that both the general and core rates could drop to 2.8 percent in January, analysts said.
Fresh food prices were performing well and expected declines in regulated tariffs and non-tradable goods, such as services, should help general inflation to fall further, they said.
"I'd expect January inflation to be around 2.8 percent, if oil prices don't rise that much," said BBV's Sebastian.
And after a flying start in January the pace of CPI growth will continue to improve during the year, analysts said. Government forecasts point to inflation ending 1997 at around 2.6 percent.
If the Bank of Spain considers inflation fever has been tamed it will have room for more interest rate cuts, totalling at least another 75 basis points next year, analysts said.
The official money market rate started the year at 9.0 percent and now stands at 6.25 percent.
